Usually don't post reviews, but having grown up with RTSes this feels like my wheelhouse.

On the face of it, 'They Are Billions' is not a bad game. It's just very, very, very basic. Complexity doesn't really start coming on until a few missions in, which wouldn't be bad if each mission didn't eat up an hour or more of your time with little engagement to keep you hooked. Comparisons to Warcraft 3 aren't without warrant, because that set a very good bar, and in comparison to Warcraft 3 it just falls very, *very* short.

The 'standard' campaign mission involves base building - you have to reach a certain population often, as well as hitting some milestones like gold income, or killing all infected units. The game forces you to expand aggressively to grow at all, and fails to give you a way to produce soldier units at the start - the stone needed isn't even within the range of the starting location, which is just tedious as hell. You also have a pitiful amount of storage to work with at the start, and once you *do* get that stone there's little to spend it on after the Barracks is built. This quickly leads to resource overflow, making it so that when you -want- to use a resource you're highly constrained because you simply cannot stockpile a lot of resources at all. You might think this is strategic, but no, it's just tedious as hell as you wait impatiently for resources to crawl back in so you can finally finish the fricken' wall. 

Furthermore, units lack tactical abilities to use. It's very much just a matter of making packs and packs of units and throwing them at the enemy, or putting them on towers along your walls. There's not a whole lot of thinking on your feet involved, it's entirely about laying down walls and towers and then moving the rest of the unit swarm around. Play more of the game, and the flaws with the units become more and more apparent. For example, each unit has it's own speed it moves at, but whereas a game like WC3 would force a selected group of units to all move at the speed of it's slowest unit, They Are Billions does *not*. This means that unit formations are difficult as hell to maintain. Units do not take automatic formations, and move at their speed regardless. This is hell, because it means unless you micromanage your group, your formation will crumble. 

This means tactics become tedious to try. For example, early on you will have Rangers and Soldiers. Your Soldiers are very chonky boys, but your Rangers - who are faster - are not. Rangers have a longer range than Soldiers do, and since you'll have Rangers left around from early scouting you'll want to use these units as support units to your Soldiers. Unfortunately, you -cannot- make the faster Rangers slow down and stay behind the Soldiers automatically. If you order the group of Soldiers and Rangers to make an attack move, the Rangers will run ahead of the tankier Soldiers, not only making them highly likely to die but getting in the way of the Soldiers who have shorter attack ranges! This becomes even worse when you get later game units, which are -even slower-, meaning you will constantly be having to micro-manage movement of units so that they stay in formation.

This is frankly unacceptable in an RTS-style game released in 2019... For comparison, in 2004, as their third game Haemimont released Nemesis of the Roman Empire. It too had a focus on huge amounts of units being on the screen, and to manage those huge armies you would take hero units, and attach generic units to them to make squads. These squads would move at the speed of the slowest unit, and remain in a formation which was strategically advantageous, and could be ordered to take up several different formations to take advantage of different unit types. Each unit also had a special quality, role in battle, and each faction had one caster unit with support abilities. These quality of life and innovative features are totally absent in They Are Billions.

Speaking of Hero Units, the Hero unit you select at the beginning of the game *only* appears in a select few exploration missions, and neither of them have any real abilities either outside of being able to find grenades and medkits to use on the maps they appear in. In WC3, maps where you had a small number of units and hero units going through a gauntlet relied on clever and timely usage of heroic abilities, unit positioning, and intelligent use of resources. 

In They Are Billions, the hero unit begins *alone* on the map, and only on a few do they pick up any extra units to command along the way. With no special abilities to use, these missions are nothing but an absolutely -miserable- and tedious game of kiting and attrition, with very, very few opportunities to get creative. Early Exploration missions have explosive barrels laying around, but later maps they just... Sort of forget to add them. A few places have environmental hazards to lure zombies through, but the game doesn't have them as *options* to pick from as much as just -requires- you to use them to progress. Some of these maps also just have no sense of restraint, throwing insufferably powerful and deadly obstacles at you which you just have to kite down over like half an hour. 

These missions also charge you with finding small collectibles hidden throughout the level to gain Research Points and Prestige - things you definitely -need- in the campaign, which are -not- highlighted or pointed out at all and can be insufferably tiny. You will almost always finish the level without finding them all, making you have to carefully pick over the level, wagging your cursor over every tiny scrap on the map, looking for a sprite that's maybe a tenth of the size of the Hero unit that you can right click on. These are the very worst parts of the game, and I hate them. Use a WeMod trainer to activate god mode, and leave combat on auto-pilot while you do something in the background. 

The third type of mission is Swarm missions. There's so little to say here, and they should have just been removed. You start in the middle of the map, you set up defenses and units, and when you're done you start, infected stream in, and if you set up your defenses right they get mulched and the map is over. Again, set up defenses and alt-tab, it's pointless to watch.

All of this is compounded by the rogue-lite element; the lack of deeper gameplay and tactics means that each and every mission is simply an exercise in patience and attrition, and if you lose you have no save state to fall back on. This means that losses don't really encourage you to rethink things to much and the daunting task of slogging back through it all again makes you not want to jump back in. The solution is hardly ever anything to do with tactics, it's everything to do with just build more walls or churn out more units. In Campaign mode this is even worse, because you're very limited building and units wise to begin with, and have to unlock move via out of mission research so you can use them during a mission. Even very -rudimentary- buildings and units like farms, towers, and soldiers must be unlocked this way. Again, use a Trainer and just give yourself infinite Research points from the start - it's more tolerable that way. 

Aesthetics wise, there's not a lot going on. An inability to rotate buildings for visual appeal dampens the colony building aspect and there's no real decorative elements. The voice acting is very poor and trite - there's no charm to what the units say and the intonation is all over the place. The maps sets are limited and dull, with few doodads to spice them up. The 'story', as much as there is one, is confused and insipid. 

Unless you just -love- Steampunk, there is nothing to recommend here. The -bones- of a good game are there, but there's no flesh to rise it above abject tedium. Use a Trainer, it's really the only way to have fun here.

This review should be read after you have read the negative review of JaylewAF11, which makes very interesting points on how this game can be ruined for you if you mismanaged some things while doing the campaign of this game. There are probably guides around the internet, but I decided I'd leave a review because why not. 

Major flaws of the campaign : 

The game allows you to spend points into a research tree to allow you to unlock new perks for your civilization. At the beginning, you will only have access to archers and wood technology, afterward you'll be able to unlock stone masonry and oil refining/foundry technology for better defenses/offense. Points are earned when successfully completed a map.

However, once you've completed a map after selecting a technology to unlock, you can't undo your decision, so if you waste points to enhance wood technology instead of rushing stone masonry and upgrading stone walls, you will be left at a fatal disadvantage as you progress in your campaign. Saying that it is a soft game over would be no understatement, so I HIGHLY recommend you unlock technologies with great care. 

if you fail a mission, the technology that you wanted to unlock will not be permanent, so if you fail a map and realize that another technology would help you complete the map (like an upgrade on soldiers DPS instead of an economy upgrade, for example), you can change the technology, provided you had enough points to unlock the other technology you're after.

The map campaign is split in between RTS map (over 2/3 of the campaign) to some solo mission that you do with a hero (hero is never present in RTS map, only in solo mission). The solo mission will require you to do a lot of kiting and hit&run tactics, carefully pulling ennemies and will take a LOT of time, so be advised that you can't rush those maps. However, those missions should always be completed first when you unlock one as you progress on the map campaign, since they also provide points to boost your tech tree. 

yes, I agree with a lot of negative reviews, you are doomed to fail some maps that have some severe ''gotcha mechanics'', and yes I felt frustrated to waste so much time building my base. You can be tempted to dump the game for a few days, but now that you know the gotcha mechanics, you might feel like me a need to take revenge and build better.

There was a mention that failing a map will provide you with less points to spend on your tech tree. I'm not sure if it's true or not, because I've never noticed a strong shortage of points to spend on my tech tree. Maybe it's because I've focused my techtree in such a ways that I didn't spend on useless techs, such as the inn or spending on wood technology,

but if I can reassure some of you, I've failed maybe 75% of the maps 1 to 3 times, and I unlocked everything I wanted to unlock, and before finishing the campaign. I still have 2 roaming waves and 2 RTS maps to finish the campaign, and all the points I will be earning is really just bonus. 

Now I redid all the maps at max difficulty (800%), and because I plan my base-building to always have some sort of backup everywhere at all time, I can do them without much trouble. 

Don't hesitate to comment on this review if you want some tips, I'd be glad to help out. Some quick tips are as followed : 

- Rush the farm and quarry technology 

- Rush stone masonry workshop to then be able to unlock soldiers and better walls afterward.

- There are 2 technologies that give you ''starter'' soldiers in addition to your starting archers. Make the archer patrol around your base while using the soldiers to clear points of interest (such as stone, iron, a cluster of wood). 

- Always wall in your most exposed building with wood walls. They're not designed to prevent your building from being destroyed by zombies, it's designed to give you some additionnal precious seconds to rapidly plan a counter if it's a little wave being sent by infected towns, and also to tank while your archers/soldiers kill the zombies. 

-Don't hesitate to use a single archer/soldier (archers move quicker) to lure zombies into a circle while the rest of your army shoot them down. 

- Rush the technologies that give you supplies each time the train comes to your base. they will allow you to build a barrack quicker and being producing soldiers. (Be careful to not make a too large army in the beginning, however. Soldiers requires a salary that will drain your gold income. Making ten soldiers and use walls to tank for them is better than making 40 soldiers that will drain your entire economy.) Only train soldiers a couple days before an annouced wave, and then you can refund them when you put them beside a barracks once you don't need them anymore. 

- The tesla tower is hands down the most useful defensive tower against large waves of weak mobs. Coupled with soldiers/snipers in towers or some wasp turret (a late tech so sniper/soldier first) that are ordered to only target the strongest zombies will take care of almost anything the game throws at you. Making 2-3 layers of stone walls will ensure that you can survive. 


However, always expect that your first line of defense may fall, so don't hesitate to build a second line of defense if you see that your first line of defense will fall, construction is quick enough that by the time your first line of defense completely fall, the construction of the 2nd line of defense will be finished. Be sure to ungarrison your soldiers/snipers to allow them to reach the second line of defense before it's too late, though. I'd also advise to make your first line of defense a certain distance from your base so you don't get overrun easily.

Good luck!

If you want zombies and INTENSE, sweaty RTS gameplay, then this game is for you! This RTS doesnt just make you hurt, it PUNISHES you. If you start a colony and it gets overrun, there is no going back to before the zombies won. You are a colony commander, its your JOB to make sure that never happens. The game mechanics are balanced and beautiful. The enemy is destructive and endless (not really... but they are on the map initially and come in waves that feel endless). If even ONE zombie gets past your outer walls, you will suffer. A single zombie can completely infect your base (quite dramatically too). Initial review after 8.3 hours:

I really wanted to like this game, but it has some of the most godawful design choices I have ever seen on an RTS.
As far as RTSs go, the game is pretty basic, but the developers tried to cover this up by adding metric tons of fake difficulty:

Having one zombie slip by your base and wreck your base by destroying one house in three hits, resulting in a snowball of zombies? Check

Having not only a metric ton of zombies in each map, but making new zombies pop in from thin air at previously cleaned up zones, resulting in the aforementioned result? Check

Having some horrible exploration missions, in which you have to clear a whole complex with a single unit, thus having a glacial pace? Check (Seriously, Starcraft did these missions better back in 1998 for Pete’s sake)

Having all these issues compounded by a forced ironman mode, meaning that if you lose a mission due to all this arbitrary BS, you have to spend one, two or more hours redoing it again? Absolutely check

And this just scratches the surface:
-	There’s no formations nor any hero abilities.
-	Mission objectives are seriously uninspired (Gather X amount of resources, have X amount of people, kill all the zombies).
-	Every mission has to be played in one specific way (i.e turtle hard, mass soldiers, mop up the map, complete the actual mission)
-	Pathfinding is all over the place, as well as targeting priorities (If the units are instructed to target the closest enemy, they will prioritize hitting an enemy a meter away, but on the other side of a wall, instead of an enemy on the same side that’s slightly further away)
-	There’s no way to highlight the relevant items that yield Empire/Research points in exploration missions, so you have to pixel hunt each box, barrel or wardrobe to make sure you’re not missing anything.

All in all, the game could be pretty good, but it’s hamstrung by some baffling design choices. Really do not recommend.


Addendum at 130 hours:

After spending 100+ hours on this heap, finishing its excuse of a campaign and getting the top achievement for score, I can safely say that I got good, but this game sure didn’t.
This campaign is now my golden standard for horrible game design. 

-	The regular missions are mind-numbingly boring, since literally all of them have the same objectives: Get a certain population, hold against all the hordes and kill all the infected. EVERY. SINGLE. TIME.
-	The exploration missions manage to be even worse. Playing these missions on Apocalypse difficulty and having to clear hundreds of zombies in each level with a couple units at most (Half the missions don’t even give you that, you can only use your hero unit) has redefined tedium for me.
-	The horde missions are unironically the least strategic missions of them all. Literally all of them, except for a couple, can be solved by just making a unit ball around your outpost and letting the infected come. Even on the highest difficulty (Hell, it’s even worse in higher difficulties, since the infected count is so high that those missions can take 10+ minutes. You can go get a drink, browse your phone or read a book; these missions require zero input).
-	There’s a lot of poor design choices masquerading as difficulty: Research is pretty badly designed, since A) You have no idea how the units or attack towers perform before unlocking them, so you’re going blind if you haven’t played Survival yet. B) There are only enough tech points for about 70% of the techs (Assuming you find every item in every exploration mission) and several techs are basically bait. This, combined with C) Being unable to respect the tech tree, means you’re pretty likely to kneecap yourself by choosing suboptimal techs on your first playthroughs and kill your progress unless you turn the difficulty way down. And if you’re playing on the highest difficulties, you pretty much have to adhere to a very specific sequence if you want to have a fighting chance.
Also, you have no idea how big hordes are going to be until the last moment, so any kind of long-term planning is impossible unless you have prior knowledge of the level. This is showcased on some levels that throw a much larger horde than what you would expect for the first horde on other levels, just to get a cheap loss (Narrow Pass, I’m looking at you).
-	As a whole, while the setting is pretty interesting, the game does next to nothing with it. The lore is borderline non-existant, there’s only two characters to speak of (The Emperor and your hero unit), there’s only 4 “cinematic sequences” (And that’s counting the one for the ending) and the blurbs describing each mission might as well be interchangeable. 
The campaign mode is basically a stretched-out Survival Mode with a tech system tacked on top. There’s absolutely no love behind its design.

The Survival mode is somewhat acceptable, but it’s nowhere near as good to carry the game nor justify its pricetag.

Can’t stress this enough: Don’t get anywhere near this game. If you want a hardcore strategy game, get Frostpunk (Sure, it’s a city builder instead of an RTS, but even then, it’s light years ahead of this).

They Are Billions is not a Tower Defence game.


I often see it compared to as such, and I think that is a bit of a lazy way to define this game. It is more akin to a classic 90s RTS with emphasis on base, economy and unit management. Oh and they are a few infected to worry about. 

It is as if the developers decided they needed to take the level "Desperate Alliance" and turn it into a video game.  Boy were they right on doing so. I never though such a basic concept, and ode to one of the greatest RTS games to ever exist, Starcraft 1, would be such a hit. Where a tower defence relies on you creating, and defeating a rush of an enemy through typical a maze, this does not abide to that rule as the hoard does not funnel in a way that a tower defence does, and they will chew through your towers / units without prejudice. 

I genuinely feel excited for the unlimited potential this game possesses. They Are Billions definitely needs some sort of workshop so I can ditch the steampunk aesthetic (not really my thing) and find something more appropriate to the Terran. 

I find it exciting to find yourself conflicted in whether or not you fortify yourself early and turtle to the best of your abilities, or you find yourself taking the fight to the infected, burning down their nests and exploiting the map as soon as you can. Both reward and punish, all depending on circumstance.

My only few gripes are: 

Spelling errors are abundant.

Pathing (reeeeeeeeeeeeeeEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE)

Sometimes the housing placement decides not to stack side by side because of "in the way" when if you redo it, it'll work. (Does that make sense?) 

Towers/ballistas not being able to shoot over trees. - perhaps its a balance thing, but common! 

Some mayor bonuses are just god awful. 


Few suggestions / ideas:

Unit variety & building - to keep things fresh.
Further advancement beyond veteran rank for soldiers.
Overhaul of soldiers in general - I personally feel they're not worth it.
Workshop support
Unit upgrades

TLDR; Game is hard but very rewarding. Do not get this if you don't want to spend hours retrying the same missions over and over. Even if you have played RTS games in the past, you will likely find this game to be uniquely challenging. My review tries to sum up the reasons that this game is challenging for a new player and why someone might not like this game, even if they like other RTS games.

None of the reviews I read prepared me for how punishing this game is. It's high quality and completely fair(contrary to what some other reviews might say, just my opinion), but this game gives you very little room for errors and you have to restart a campaign mission from the start if you fail, as you can't reload a save. You will probably be dead before you know that you are dead because failing to prepare for an attack can result in your base getting wiped.

to be clear, I don't think this is the hardest RTS or is some ultra-hardcore elite challenge, just that the learning curve is pretty steep and that you probably are going to lose a whole bunch before you win.

The campaign sets the tone for its difficulty immediately. The first two campaign missions aren't that bad, and they become pretty tough immediately after. You can always lower the difficulty but I don't think that will necessarily help.

The difficulty setting seems very deceptive to me, because playing on 100% challenging might have more zombies with higher health than lower difficulties, but no matter what, if one zombie gets past your initial defenses and attacks your housing, that results in more zombies spawning from the destroyed housing, quickly leading into a downward spiral, which you have to watch as your base slowly gets torn apart. You can't even surrender a mission to restart, you can just watch it fall apart. When you select the mission to retry it, there is a counter to tell you how many times you have failed.

The campaign also has 'hero missions' where you control a small group of units and clear out an area, and there are also 'horde missions', which are like a tower defense game. I don't care much for these missions but they are not meant to be the focus of the campaign, and they are generally shorter than retrying the build missions while you learn the game.

Overall I really like it but the learning curve is steep and the time investment feels pretty large due to the long missions and many resets. The big 3 points for why you might not like this game
-Not having saves is brutal
-Missions are long and you may have to reset after an hour
-Easy to fail regardless of difficulty
-You are forced to watch your base get destroyed and your spirit gets crushed as you look at the number of times you failed that mission.

The dopamine hit when you beat a level is [i]mint[/i], however.

This is truly the Dark Souls of RTS games

Skilled players make this game look easy

Survive til day 90
Have 3 concentric rings of double walls and gun-turrets at each instance, 1300 gold economy, overflow of resources, lifes good
One single passage where no zombie has ever set foot during the ENTIRE game, place 1 soldier there
Name soldier Bob,
Proceed to absolutely destroy the final hordes in the midst of intense lags
Finally its over, Im gonna unlock the next map now, 
Suddenly hears screams from inner colony,
See zombies grow exponentially as they infect each household...
*Click on Bob*
"Sorry sir, I was just cleaning my weapon"
F**k you Bob

10/10 would not trust Bob again

On a more serious note, this game is amazing and incredibly addicting, every restart is completely different and you get better with each attempt, you need to be able to adapt to the resource locations and horde locations. Although 7 entrances to your base from the start is not a good sign, if you expand aggressively you will be able to narrow that down to fewer choke points, this game is very rewarding in that sense, you can turn the worst starting situation around, even in your favour.

No save game in the campaign halts all momentum.
A weak spot in your wall appears 40 minutes in a level? Game over. One zombie attacking a tent turns into 3 turns into 9 turns into 27. Its always game over.
Patch that wall next game. Another weak spot 70 minutes in? Game over. Rinse and repeat.

I enjoy the playstyle. Its engrossing... The first time. Retreading the same steps in the same level 3-4 times for 30-60 minutes at a time hoping something goes differently the 5th time is monotony.

I value my free time. This game does not.

I'm sure veterens have figured out a way to 'game' the system on high difficulty, but repetitively playing over the same scenarios for X hours until the game mechanics click for me isn't doing it here.

If I had 25+ hours in the game already to learn what I need to to play the game, I'm sure I'd enjoy it. But playing through 30 minutes in one level only to have a strategic mistake spell my doom at 35 minutes, forcing me to repeat the same first 30 minutes over only again for something else to do me in at 40 minutes just kills my desire to progress. (Emphatically, with no save feature available even in the campaign.)

I understand the devs' intent to create a game with a sense of caution and purpose in one's actions. I appreciate that. But omitting a save feature or even a checkpoint is alienating. Even checkpoints throughout a mission would keep me going. But that isn't the case here.

*Update: After 25 hours of gameplay my feelings haven't changed. If the game wasn't Iron-Man-Only mode I would have invested much more time.

There are many positive comments detailing what's good about the game (most of which I agree with) so my review is to add some perspective for prospective buyers of the game in its current state. If you're half-decent at RTS games, the gameplay gets pretty stale after several run throughs with the limited content and fairly simple game mechanics. You'd quickly realize that there are only a handful of units that are worth considering and getting a critical number of these units to just steamroll through all the zombies is basically one of very few ways to win. The limited "microing" mechanic normally associated with RTS games make the skill ceiling even lower and limits playstyle to basically patrol move (not attack move because it's currently bugged but that's another story).

So on to the topic of bugs. There's lots of them, most of which might not negatively affect the gaming experience of new or lower skilled player but will definitely affect gameplay for those who are more experienced or skilled at RTS. Case in point, game can often become frustratingly unresponsive to user input trying to micro a single unit or small number of units i.e. navigating a unit through a crowd of zombies is only reliably done by spamming 'M' key for move and left-clicking where you want the unit to go because just right-click moving is so clunky that it can often get your unit killed. And good luck trying to select certain units in a group especially in critical situations.

But it's early access you say, give the devs time to work on the bugs you say. Here's the thing. It's been three months since the game release and there's been very limited communication coming from the devs. They stopped responding to comments on their own community page a month into early access release and even then they seem to ignore comments regarding bugs that many people seem to be experiencing and giving vague canned responses to things most people don't care about. Of the two or so development updates, all signs point to the dev team just sticking to their plan to add a campaign and be done with the game. The community challenges the devs added have been a joke--absolutely no new content as it's just survival mode on normal difficulty where players just plop buildings on every tile of the maps to try to get the highest score. It's not even enjoyable, it's tedious. The six new "Wonder" buildings don't seem to add any real content to the stale gameplay--just luxury buildings that require a lot of resources that will add to final score. Yawn.

Closing in on 1,000 hours and still keep going. Something about how challenging this game is keeps me coming back for more. Would be nice if the devs added some new content but guess they are satisfied with what it is.

I haven't finished the campaign (51%), but I just can't go further. Not because it is impossible, but for how punishing this game is. I have playing in difficulty 100% the whole way, I admit it was challenging, and emotionally rewarding every time I cleared a mission.

Here's my biggest disappointment. When you lose, you feel that you have just lost 2 hours of your life for nothing, due to inadvertence for most of the case. 1 mistake, and your entire game is ruined. You really need to do the right decisions with a reaaally narrow margin for errors. You can't really play the way you want. It is always the same loop.

The hero mission is meaningless and boring as hell. I always play them at 25% difficulty (less enemies) because it is such a hassle to take down hundreds of infected one by one (if you don't have grenades). Same here, you only have one character, and if your hero dies, you have to redo the entire boring mission from start. I was about to complete a hero mission when a Harpy showed up and killed me in 2 hits. OMG, no waaaaay I am redoing this stupid mission. I understand very well the meaning of punishment in video games, but not this one, it was so useless and unfair.

Pretty great game overall, but for me personally failed to go to distance. 

     It was great exploring the mechanics of the game but every mission starts to feel reeeaaaal samey. Clear some zombies, put some walls up, expand, resist a wave, - repeat. Northguard suffers the same repetition for different reasons.
     The lack of save options is a huge detriment to the game and replay value of the title, you make 1 mistake somewhere and you'll lose the entire settlement, which is fun. I like that, what I don't like is starting the mission over and repeating the same tedious settlement expansion for a mission. Not fun, ever.
     The game doesn't benefit enough from random maps and needs more focus. Overall, I had fun with this game. But when I was done. I was done. Don't think I'll be coming back until the next game.
